e.t: Abital is a personal name, rendered “Abital” or “Avital.” It functions as the name of a particular person rather than as a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: in 2 Samuel 3:4 and 1 Chronicles 3:3. The available wording identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role in either passage.

This adjective describes something that cannot be eaten or is not suitable as food. It gives a plain, practical description of food’s condition or usefulness, rather than naming a person, action, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 24:22. That reference identifies its occurrence, while the exact force there depends on the surrounding verse text. Its core meaning is “uneatable; not good for food.”

This word means “loving” and, as a noun, names the quality or expression of being loving. It refers to love as a recognizable attitude or disposition rather than functioning as an action word. In the Greek Old Testament, including its deuterocanonical books, it occurs 17 times in 16 verses. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains loving concern directed toward another.

This noun refers to a “holy place” or “sanctuary”—a place set apart as sacred. In the Greek Old Testament, it names a sacred location, not merely a quality of holiness. The word occurs four times, appearing once in Leviticus and three times in Psalms. Its precise reference in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a holy place or sanctuary.

Aingadois, also rendered Enggathis, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek text, but the available information does not establish which one. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Sirach 24:14. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from that passage’s surrounding context and the wider biblical setting.

This LXX verb means “make to hear,” describing an action that brings someone or something into hearing. It is a verb, so it expresses what is done rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, across passages in Judges, Psalms, Jeremiah, Sirach, and Song of Songs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes something at the highest or most prominent point—the “pinnacle” or “apex.” It can identify a chief, elevated position rather than something ordinary or low. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 28:16. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea is a prominent topmost point or leading position.

This Greek LXX verb means “taken,” describing someone or something being seized, captured, or carried away. It presents taking as an action rather than as a person, object, or quality. The word occurs 29 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing regular use across these writings. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what or whom the surrounding sentence says is taken. The supplied references include Exodus 22:8, Proverbs 11:6, and several passages in Isaiah.

This adjective describes something gloomy—marked by darkness, heaviness, or a bleak quality. It is a descriptive word rather than an action or title, so it identifies the character or appearance of what it modifies. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is clearly “gloomy.”

“Impede” means to hinder or hold something back so that it cannot move forward freely. As a verb, this word describes an action that interferes with progress rather than simply naming a fixed condition. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs three times: once in Wisdom and twice in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what is being hindered, but its central idea remains preventing or slowing progress.

Anan is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is presented as the name itself: “Anan.” It occurs 16 times in the LXX, across 16 verses, including passages in 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the particular person identified by Anan must be determined from each passage’s context.

This adjective describes something that cannot be brought to an end—something interminable. It presents duration, extent, or continuation as having no clear stopping point, rather than merely lasting a long time. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines what continuing or unending thing is being described.

Armaith is a proper name, rendered “Armaith,” with “Armeth” given as an alternate form. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 19:36. Because it is a name rather than a common noun or action word, its meaning is primarily its identifying function: it designates a particular named entity in that passage. The available information does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything more specific about the name’s referent.

This adjective describes something that is “without roots” or “uprooted”—no longer firmly planted or established. It can refer to a plant that has been pulled from the ground, or more generally to something deprived of its foundation. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Job 31:8, and its translated rendering there is “uprooted.” The surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely how the image functions in that passage.

This verb means to “endeavor”: to make a deliberate effort toward something. It describes purposeful striving rather than a passive wish, presenting effort as an action someone undertakes. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:4. That reference identifies where the word appears, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the particular situation. Its basic sense remains focused on active effort or earnest attempt.

This Greek LXX noun means “anklebone,” the bony joint connecting the foot and lower leg. It names a specific part of the body rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Zechariah 11:16. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a literal reference to the anklebone.

This word means “neck” or “throat,” referring to the part of the body between the head and shoulders. It is a noun used for this bodily area, whether described as a single neck or as necks. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in Joshua, 2 Chronicles, Psalms, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Apharsaioi, also rendered Afarsei, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a named people or designation in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once, in Ezra 4:9. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise reference cannot be described further, but its basic function is to identify the named party represented by this name.

This noun means “departure,” referring to the act of leaving or going away. It names a movement from one place or situation to another rather than describing the person who leaves. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 7:18. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what departure is meant there, but the word itself carries the straightforward sense of leaving or departing.

Baithacharma, also rendered Vethakharma, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. The word identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Jeremiah 6:1. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its specific referent cannot be explained further here; the lexical evidence establishes the name itself, not the contextual significance of its appearance.

This Greek LXX noun means “missile.” It refers to a weapon sent toward a target, such as something launched or thrown in battle. The word appears 41 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it normally names a physical object rather than an action or quality. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a missile used against a target.

Bosorra, also given as Vosorra, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Genesis, 1 Chronicles, Job, and 1 Maccabees. Because the available information provides no verse text or surrounding context, its precise reference in each passage cannot be explained here; the secure meaning is the name itself.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Bōla” or “Vola.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:3. Because it is a name and no surrounding verse text is available here, its precise identity must be understood from that passage’s context. The name is preserved as a distinct Greek LXX word and should not be treated as a general term with a broader abstract meaning.

This verb means “happen” or “become”: it describes something coming to pass or entering a new state. It can refer to an event that occurs, a condition that develops, or something that comes into being. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly, occurring 1,971 times across 1,805 verses, so its precise sense is determined by the sentence and surrounding passage. Its earliest recorded use is in Genesis 1:3, and it continues throughout the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books.

This Greek LXX verb means “coward”: it describes acting with cowardice or shrinking back from courage. As a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming a person who is a coward. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 5:41. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is the act of being cowardly. This Greek LXX verb means “bind round”: to wrap or fasten something around another object. It describes an action rather than a person, place, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 9:11. The available lexical meaning clearly establishes the word’s basic sense, while the precise object being bound and the force of the action depend on the verse’s surrounding text.

This Greek LXX verb means “extend”: to reach or stretch outward or onward. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Wisdom 7:24, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic idea remains the movement of something across or toward a further point.

This noun means “evaluation”—the act of examining or assessing something to determine its quality, fitness, or worth. It refers to a process of testing rather than to the person who performs it or the result reached afterward. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 6:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage, but the central idea remains careful assessment or examination.

gl: captive of the spear; taken in war
d: captive of the spear; taken in war

e.t: This adjective describes someone captured in battle—a “captive of the spear” or one “taken in war.” It portrays a person who has been seized as a result of armed conflict, rather than someone who freely chooses a situation. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a war captive.

This adjective means “subject,” describing someone or something placed under another’s authority or rule. It identifies a condition of submission rather than naming an action. The word appears 47 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so it is used across a broad range of passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and subject being described.

This adjective describes someone or something as “full of ill-will” or “hostile.” It refers to an attitude or disposition marked by opposition, unfriendly intent, or active hostility. The word appears five times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Esther and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what person or thing it describes and the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb expresses coming to understand something—to realize it or have an idea of it. It describes an act of knowing or recognizing, rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word appears 878 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so it is a broadly used verb for awareness and understanding. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word means “mercy”—compassionate kindness shown toward someone in need or distress. It can describe mercy itself or function in a sentence to express merciful action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 292 times, showing that mercy is a widely used biblical idea rather than a rare expression. Its clearest English rendering is “mercy,” and the surrounding passage determines how that mercy is being expressed in a particular verse.

Eliatha is a proper name referring to a person named Eliatha. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in 1 Chronicles 25:27. The available lexical definition gives the name itself, “Eliatha,” rather than describing an action, quality, or general concept. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be explained further; its basic meaning is its use as a personal designation.

This Greek LXX verb means “do business”: to engage in buying, selling, or other commercial activity. It describes the practical act of conducting trade rather than naming a person or place. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in passages from Genesis through Amos. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains commercial activity or trade.

This Greek LXX verb means to “reach” or “arrive at” a place or destination. It describes coming as far as a particular point, emphasizing arrival rather than merely setting out or traveling. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Judges 5:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is movement that successfully comes to a designated place.

This Greek LXX verb means “impose as a burden”—to place a load, responsibility, or demand upon someone. Its central idea is making something burdensome for another person, rather than simply carrying it oneself. The word appears once in the Greek LXX, in Nehemiah 13:15. The precise force of that occurrence belongs to its surrounding verse and passage, but the word’s basic meaning is to burden or load someone with an imposed demand.

This Greek LXX verb means “prop up” or “steady”: it describes giving support so that someone or something is held firm rather than left to fall or waver. It can refer to physical support, but the basic idea is strengthening or stabilizing. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing across books such as Genesis, Judges, 2 Samuel, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom it describes.

This verb means “become stinking” or “putrefy,” describing something that develops a foul odor as it decays. It refers to a change or condition rather than simply naming an unpleasant smell. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Exodus. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains becoming foul and rotten.

Esdrikam, also rendered Ezthrikam, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 1 Chronicles 9:44 and once in 2 Chronicles 28:7. The available lexical information identifies it as a personal name, but does not provide an additional ordinary meaning or explanation of the name itself. Its particular significance in either passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This word is a proper name, referring to “Esthaōlaioi; Esthaolei.” It is not presented as an ordinary descriptive word or action, but as the name of a particular group or designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 2:53. Because no verse text or broader contextual evidence is available here, the name’s precise reference must be understood from that passage rather than from the name alone.

Eschōl, also rendered Eskhol, is a proper name used for a person or place identified by that name. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Genesis 14. The word itself functions as a name rather than a general description, action, or quality. Its precise referent in each occurrence depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical meaning provided is simply “Eschōl” or “Eskhol.”

This adjective describes something musical or rhythmical—marked by pleasing sound, ordered movement, or a harmonious quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, in Wisdom 17:17, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. The word focuses on the character of a sound or movement rather than naming a person, action, or object by itself. Its exact force in that verse depends on the sentence where it occurs.

This verb means to “use words of good omen”—to speak in a way associated with favorable signs or wishes. It describes an action involving speech rather than a person, object, or place. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 5:64. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly how the action functions in that passage.

Ephrathaios is a proper name, also given as “Efratheos.” It is a name used in the Greek Old Testament rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Ruth 1:2. Because the available lexical meaning is a name and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its specific reference must be read from that passage.

This proper noun identifies a person called a “Zaboulōnitēs,” also rendered “Zavulonitis.” It functions as a personal or group designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Judges 12, at Judges 12:11 and Judges 12:12. The word’s precise reference in each verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the identifying name itself.

This verb describes becoming tranquil or keeping quiet. It points to settled stillness rather than agitation or disturbance, and it can describe someone or something remaining calm. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 43 times, so its basic idea is used across a range of passages. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on quiet behavior, peaceful conditions, or cessation of disturbance; the core meaning remains calmness and quiet.

This noun means “noise” or “sound”—something heard by the ear. It can refer broadly to an audible sound rather than naming one particular kind of noise. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 14 times, so its meaning is established across multiple passages rather than being limited to a single setting. The surrounding verse determines whether it describes a human, natural, or other audible sound.

This verb means “touch”: to make contact with someone or something. It describes the act of reaching or coming into physical contact, rather than merely seeing or approaching. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 19:12. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but its basic meaning remains direct physical contact.

This Greek LXX noun means “hick,” referring to a person described with that label. It functions as a name or designation for a person rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Proverbs 6:8. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains a reference to a “hick.”

This Greek LXX noun means “temple,” referring to a place set apart for worship and sacred service. It names the temple as a physical location rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 60 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages from Chronicles, Ezekiel, and the Maccabean books. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on how the surrounding passage presents that temple.

This Greek LXX noun means “appearance,” referring to how something presents itself or is seen. It names the visible form or outward presentation of something, rather than describing an action. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Jeremiah and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains an appearance or visible form.

Iōsēpos, also rendered Iosipos, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning in a sentence is primarily the person’s name. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times: twice in 1 Maccabees and twice in 2 Maccabees. The surrounding verse is needed to identify which person is meant in each occurrence.

This noun means “caterpillar,” naming a particular creature. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it occurs five times, in Nehemiah, Joel, and Amos. Its clearest English rendering is “caterpillar,” and its repeated appearance in Joel supports understanding it as a creature-name rather than an abstract description or action. The word functions as a noun: it identifies the creature being mentioned. Its precise role in any individual verse depends on the surrounding text.

This Greek LXX verb means “go down” or “sink,” describing movement from a higher position to a lower one, including going beneath or descending into something. Its basic sense can apply to a person, object, or movement downward, depending on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus, Jeremiah, Amos, and Micah. These occurrences show a consistent action of descending rather than an abstract idea. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the immediate context.

This verb means “study; learn about.” It describes giving attention to something in order to understand it or gain knowledge of it. As an action word, it focuses on the process of examining or becoming informed, rather than merely noticing something briefly. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs seven times, including passages in Genesis, Leviticus, Job, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being examined and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means to carry off as booty—that is, to seize people or possessions as spoils after conquest. It describes an act of taking away what has been captured, rather than simply moving or carrying something. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers 21:1 and Judges 2:14, so its precise force in either passage comes from the surrounding context. Its central idea remains the removal of spoil by taking it as booty.

This verb describes someone who is “easily cajoled”—readily persuaded by coaxing or pressure. It presents a person as lacking firmness when another tries to influence the choices they make. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Proverbs 7:22, but the available information does not include the verse text, so its broader lexical sense is the proper focus here. Its verbal function highlights what happens to a person who is readily drawn along by another's persuasion.

This verb means “punish”: to impose a penalty or corrective judgment on someone for wrongdoing. It describes an action carried out against a person, rather than a general condition or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 21 times, most often in Wisdom and also in the Maccabean books. Its exact force in any passage depends on who is acting, who receives the punishment, and the surrounding statement.

The word means “pummel”—to strike someone repeatedly and forcefully. As a verb, it describes a physical action rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented by this lexical entry, it occurs twice, once in Amos 2:7 and once in Malachi 3:5. Those references locate its two uses, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the precise force of each occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun means “barley,” the grain named in passages across the Old Testament and once in the deuterocanonical books. It is used as an ordinary agricultural term, appearing 35 times in this LXX corpus and in 33 verses. The word occurs in Genesis, Leviticus, Ruth, Samuel, and other books, showing a recurring reference to barley rather than an abstract quality or action.

This word means “talk” or “speak”: it describes the act of expressing words aloud. It is a verb used for ordinary human speech and for words spoken in important conversations throughout the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books. It occurs 1,082 times in this corpus, so its basic sense is broad and frequent rather than limited to one special kind of speech. Its precise force in any passage depends on what is being said and who is speaking.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Lousamēncha” or “Lusaminkha.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general concept; its function is to identify an individual. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:10. The available information establishes the name and its single occurrence, but without the verse text it does not establish further details about the person or the role the name plays in that passage.

Maouda, also rendered Mautha, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or idea. It identifies a named person or entity in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once, in Ezra 2:52. The available information establishes the name and its location, but the name alone does not explain the person’s identity or role; that requires the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun means “member.” It identifies an individual member, functioning as a naming word rather than an action, description, or command. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs 11 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. The listed occurrences span books such as Job, Ezekiel, Sirach, and Maccabees, so its use is repeated but not frequent. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding text.

This Greek LXX verb means “mingle with”—to mix or associate with someone or something. It describes joining together rather than remaining separate. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Isaiah and once in Hosea, so its central idea is clear even though its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. It is a practical word describing mixture or shared association.

This word means “lead,” the heavy metal. It is a noun naming a physical material, not an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears 11 times, including passages associated with Exodus, Numbers, Job, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its uses include lead as a tangible substance, so the surrounding sentence determines whether it is being mentioned as an object, material, or part of an image. The word’s basic meaning remains the metal itself.

Mochati is a proper name, rendered as “Mochati” or “Mokhati,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 47:8. Because a proper name identifies rather than defines a general concept, its exact referent must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage; the name itself does not provide an additional ordinary meaning.

Moōcha is a proper name, rendered also as “Mookha.” It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. The name occurs four times in the Greek LXX, all in 1 Chronicles. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise family or personal connection in each occurrence cannot be stated here. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the personal name Moōcha, preserved as a name in these genealogical and historical records.

Naeth is a proper name, rendered “Naeth,” rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 31:13. The lexical information preserves the name itself but does not identify from the name alone whether Naeth refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its exact referent must therefore be determined from the surrounding verse and passage.

Nemrim is a proper name, rendered as “Nemrim,” rather than a general word describing an action, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Isaiah 15:6. Because the available lexical meaning is simply the name itself and no verse text is provided here, its precise referent must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context. The name should therefore be retained as Nemrim when reading this occurrence.

Omachathi is a proper name, also rendered “Omakhathi.” It identifies a specific named subject rather than expressing a general quality, action, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Deuteronomy 3:14. The supplied lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide a separate underlying meaning or explain the person or place it identifies. Its precise reference in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means to provide someone with weapons or to arm them. It describes the action of equipping a person for defense or conflict, rather than merely possessing weapons. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 14:32. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the supplying or giving of arms.

This word means “never”. It is an adverb that expresses absolute refusal, denial, or the absence of an event at any time. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears four times, including passages from Exodus, 1 Kings, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its force is stronger than simply saying something has not happened yet: it points to no time at all. The surrounding sentence determines what action, condition, or possibility is being ruled out.

The word means “almighty,” a noun used as a title for one understood to possess supreme power. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used chiefly as a designation for God. Its central emphasis is greatness of power and authority, rather than a particular action or quality. This word occurs 173 times in the Greek LXX corpus, showing that it is a well-established title throughout these Scriptures.

This Greek LXX verb means “act unlawfully.” It describes a person’s action as unlawful or contrary to what is permitted. The word appears 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Job, Psalms, and 4 Maccabees. Its basic emphasis is on doing what violates a recognized law or rule, while the precise force in any verse depends on that passage’s surrounding wording.

This noun means “pirate,” referring to a person who attacks or robs at sea. It names a kind of lawless sea raider rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs three times, in Job and Hosea. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains a pirate or maritime robber.

This noun refers to the content of something or to what encloses it. Its central idea concerns what is contained within a thing, or the boundary or surrounding area that contains it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 25 times across 25 verses, so its precise sense in a particular passage depends on whether the context emphasizes the contents or the enclosing space. It is distinct from a Greek New Testament word and belongs specifically to the LXX vocabulary.

This word means “bitter herb,” referring to a plant characterized by a sharp, unpleasant taste. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and occurs twice, in Exodus 12:8 and Numbers 9:11. Its meaning identifies the herb itself rather than an emotion or attitude. The word’s precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and instructions, but its basic sense remains a bitter-tasting herb.

This noun refers to prostitution or depravity—conduct marked by sexual unfaithfulness or moral corruption. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it appears 48 times, showing that it is a recurring term for seriously corrupt sexual or moral behavior. Its use includes both direct references to prostitution and figurative descriptions of unfaithfulness. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding context, but its central sense remains prostitution or depravity.

This verb means “proper,” describing what is fitting or appropriate in a given situation. It presents something as suitable rather than out of place. The word appears ten times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Psalms, Sirach, 1 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Because it is a verb, it expresses the action or state of being proper, rather than naming a person or object. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “denounce beforehand.” It describes making a denunciation known in advance, before the matter fully unfolds. As an action word, it focuses on the prior act of announcing the denunciation rather than merely describing a person or thing. It occurs once in the Greek text of Wisdom, at Wisdom 18:19. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “report,” referring to the act of making information known or bringing it forward for others to hear. It is a Greek LXX word found once in the deuterocanonical corpus, in 2 Maccabees 11:36. Because the available lexical meaning is brief and the verse text is not included here, the surrounding passage is needed to determine exactly what information is being reported in that occurrence.
